title: S*LM

sourceEvidence.excerpt: S*LM accepts the demonstrated value of scale while rejecting the assumption that one general model should own every operation in an agentic workflow. A useful agent must interpret an underspecified request, preserve prohibitions, resolve entities, retrieve authoritative state, calculate, plan, call tools, validate effects, remember outcomes, and explain what happened. These operations demand different kinds of competence and carry different risks. The book therefore changes the unit of analysis from an isolated model to the complete controlled process that moves language into consequential state changes. Its guiding question is not how small a universal assistant can become, but how much generality each role actually requires. The star in S*LM is a wildcard. A component may be small, specialized, symbolic, or combine these properties; the label describes a system family, not a claim that planners and solvers are language models. Smallness is deployment-relative: it matters when a model crosses into local execution, inexpensive high-volume serving, lower latency, offline use, or proximity to private data. Specialization can concern task, domain, interface, policy, or hardware, each with different validation and maintenance costs. Symbolic structure begins when representations and operations can be inspected independently of next-token probability: schemas, queries, constraints, plans, programs, databases, or proofs. sourceEvidence.locator: Minimum sufficient generality and progressive compilation
sourceEvidence.excerpt: The programme’s design objective is minimum sufficient generality, not minimum parameter count. Every role should declare an input distribution, output contract, failure envelope, authority level, and escalation path before a model is selected. A closed intent set may need only a classifier; flexible schema-bounded arguments may justify a compact generative model; exact search may belong to a solver; unfamiliar synthesis may justify a frontier model. The central research hypothesis is that recurring agent trajectories can be progressively compiled. Early systems use general models heavily to interpret requests and generate examples. As stable subproblems become visible, organizations can convert them into labelled datasets, adapters, validators, deterministic functions, symbolic procedures, and versioned capability packages. This migration is not assumed to work everywhere. Semantic dive

Decomposition begins at semantic intake. Requests contain goals, entities, constraints, ambiguity, language variation, and prohibitions whose survival must be tested through the whole workflow rather than at an isolated classification step. Transformations such as translation, summarization, normalization, extraction, and redaction need explicit invariants—especially around negation, modality, quantities, temporal order, exceptions, and uncertainty. Formalization then converts accepted interpretations into schemas, queries, plans, logic, or code, but compiler success must remain separate from semantic fidelity. Planning and tool use should yield governed state transitions, not merely plausible action text.
